claim: The Zebrafish Mutation Project (ZMP) aims to identify disruptive alleles in all of the more than 26,000 genes in the vertebrate genome.
source: Systematic initiatives such as the Zebrafish Mutation Project (ZMP) aim to identify disruptive alleles in all of the more than 26,000 genes in the vertebrate genome and make these available to the scientific community (Kettleborough et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kettleborough et al., 2013, which provides external evidence for the ZMP's goals.

claim: The ZMP characterizes all alleles for approximately 20 gross structural and behavioral phenotypes at 5 days post fertilization.
source: For example, the ZMP characterizes all alleles for ~20 gross structural and behavioral phenotypes (e.g. axis length, movement, etc.) at 5 days post fertilization (dpf) (Dooley et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dooley et al., 2013, which provides external evidence for the ZMP's characterization approach.

claim: Phenotyping in large studies is often non-quantitative and restricted to features easily observed by eye.
source: As a result, phenotyping in large studies is often non-quantitative and restricted to features easily observed by eye.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' inference from the state of the field and the limitations of current approaches.

claim: Optical projection tomography (OPT) is a 3D imaging technique operating on the same principle as X-ray computed tomography but utilizing visible radiation instead of X-rays.
source: Image acquisition is accomplished using optical projection tomography (OPT), a 3D imaging technique operating on the same principle as X-ray computed tomography but utilizing visible radiation instead of X-rays (Reynaud, 2013; Sharpe et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Reynaud, 2013 and Sharpe et al., 2002, which provide external evidence for the principles of OPT.

claim: OPT is capable of imaging both absorption of transmitted light and emitted fluorescence.
source: OPT is capable of imaging both absorption of transmitted light and emitted fluorescence (Wang and Wang, 2007), making it ideal for deep-phenotyping of chromogenic WISH.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang and Wang, 2007, which provides external evidence for OPT's imaging capabilities.

claim: Acquisition times for OPT are extremely short when high-contrast stains are used.
source: Compared to fluorescence imaging techniques, acquisition times for OPT are extremely short when high-contrast stains are used, a crucial requirement for large-scale analysis.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of OPT's performance characteristics compared to other imaging modalities.

claim: The authors have previously described a high-throughput OPT system to quantify craniofacial skeletons in zebrafish embryos using the Alcian blue histological stain.
source: We have previously described a high-throughput OPT system to quantify craniofacial skeletons in zebrafish embryos using the Alcian blue histological stain (Pardo-Martin et al., 2010, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work (Pardo-Martin et al., 2010, 2013).

claim: Fezf2 is an evolutionarily conserved transcription factor that plays critical roles in neurogenesis and cell fate specification in organisms ranging from Drosophila to mammals.
source: Fezf2 is an evolutionarily conserved transcription factor that plays critical roles in neurogenesis and cell fate specification in organisms ranging from Drosophila to mammals (Eckler and Chen, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eckler and Chen, 2014, which provides external evidence for Fezf2's evolutionary conservation and function.

claim: In mice, Fezf2 is expressed in forebrain neural progenitors and postmitotic glutamatergic projection neurons in layers 5 and 6 of the neocortex.
source: In mice, Fezf2 is expressed in forebrain neural progenitors and postmitotic glutamatergic projection neurons in layers 5 and 6 of the neocortex (Inoue et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Inoue et al., 2004, which provides external evidence for Fezf2 expression patterns in mice.

claim: Fezf2 knockout mice show a striking loss of corticospinal motor neurons and other closely related subcerebral projection neurons in cortical layer 5, which are replaced by callosal projection neurons.
source: Knockout mice show a striking loss of corticospinal motor neurons and other closely related subcerebral projection neurons in cortical layer 5, which are replaced by callosal projection neurons (Molyneaux et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2005a, 2005b, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Molyneaux et al., 2005 and Chen et al., 2005a, 2005b, 2008, which provide external evidence for the phenotype of Fezf2 knockout mice.

claim: Developmental expression of Fezf2 is similar in fish and mammals.
source: Although developmental expression of Fezf2 is similar in fish and mammals (Berberoglu et al., 2009; Blechman et al., 2007; Levkowitz et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2005a, 2005b; Hirata et al., 2004; Molyneaux et al., 2005), previously reported loss-of-function phenotypes differ in important aspects.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Berberoglu et al., 2009; Blechman et al., 2007; Levkowitz et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2005a, 2005b; Hirata et al., 2004; Molyneaux et al., 2005) that provide external evidence for similar Fezf2 expression patterns across species.

claim: The fezf2m808 mutant (also known as too few) is thought to be a hypomorphic loss-of-function allele.
source: The function of fezf2 in zebrafish has been extensively studied using the fezf2m808 mutant (also known as too few), which is thought to be a hypomorphic loss-of-function allele (Jeong et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jeong et al., 2006, which provides external evidence for the nature of the fezf2m808 allele.

claim: Early developmental deficits in zebrafish fezf2 mutants have only been reported in diencephalon, particularly in dopaminergic, serotonergic, oxytocinergic-like, and GABAergic populations.
source: In contrast to knockout mice, where fezf2 defects are seen in the glutamatergic projection neurons of the telencephalon-derived neocortex, early developmental deficits in zebrafish embryos have only been reported in diencephalon, particularly in dopaminergic (DA), serotonergic (5-HT), oxytocinergic-like, and GABAergic populations (Blechman et al., 2007; Rink and Guo, 2004; Yang et al., 2012; Guo et al., 1999; Levkowitz et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Blechman et al., 2007; Rink and Guo, 2004; Yang et al., 2012; Guo et al., 1999; Levkowitz et al., 2003) that provide external evidence for previously reported zebrafish fezf2 phenotypes.

claim: Adult fezf2 mutant zebrafish have significantly smaller telencephalons.
source: Support for the latter possibility comes from the finding that adult fezf2 mutant zebrafish have significantly smaller telencephalons, in spite of the fact that early developmental defects are reported in the diencephalon (Berberoglu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berberoglu et al., 2014, which provides external evidence for the adult telencephalon phenotype in fezf2 mutants.

claim: The telencephalon appears grossly normal at two weeks post fertilization in fezf2 mutants.
source: Although the telencephalon appears grossly normal at two weeks post fertilization, we speculated that deep-phenotyping might uncover earlier abnormalities.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' inference from the literature and their own observations.

claim: Formaldehyde fixation renders normally transparent zebrafish embryos optically dense.
source: Because formaldehyde fixation renders normally transparent zebrafish embryos optically dense, high-resolution OPT requires tissue clearing techniques to reduce light scattering and maximize transparency.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the effects of formaldehyde fixation on tissue optical properties.

claim: Immersion in a mixture of benzyl alcohol and benzyl benzoate (BABB) is a simple and rapid solvent-based clearing technique.
source: Immersion in a mixture of benzyl alcohol and benzyl benzoate (BABB) is a simple and rapid solvent-based clearing technique.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about BABB as a tissue clearing method.

claim: BABB has a refractive index of 1.559.
source: BABB's hydrophobicity and high refractive index (RI; 1.559) render samples optically transparent, making deeper structures accessible for high-resolution 3D imaging (Becker et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Becker et al., 2012, which provides external evidence for BABB's refractive index.

claim: Aluminosilicate glass has a refractive index of 1.538.
source: In order to match the RI of BABB, we load samples into an aluminosilicate glass capillary (RI = 1.538) instead of a borosilicate capillary (RI = 1.474), which is immersed in a BABB-filled glass cuvette to achieve RI matching between the inside and outside (Figure 1A; details in Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is stated as a fact in the manuscript and is based on the authors' knowledge of material properties.

claim: Borosilicate glass has a refractive index of 1.474.
source: In order to match the RI of BABB, we load samples into an aluminosilicate glass capillary (RI = 1.538) instead of a borosilicate capillary (RI = 1.474), which is immersed in a BABB-filled glass cuvette to achieve RI matching between the inside and outside (Figure 1A; details in Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is stated as a fact in the manuscript and is based on the authors' knowledge of material properties.

claim: The OPT platform can acquire 360 color images with a pixel resolution of approximately 1.5 µm and a rotation time of approximately 12 seconds.
source: For each specimen, we acquire 360 color images with a pixel resolution of ~1.5 µm and a rotation time of ~12 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the authors' experiments with the OPT platform.

claim: The registration strategy utilizes both the dark blue chromogenic in situ stain and a faint red SYTOX Green counterstain.
source: Our registration strategy is described in detail in Materials and methods and utilizes both the dark blue chromogenic in situ stain (which can be clearly visualized in the red or green channels of an RGB image and highlights internal morphology) and a faint red SYTOX Green counterstain (which can be visualized in the blue or green channels and highlights surface features that are common to all embryos).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach and is based on their experimental design.

claim: The registration algorithms produce alignments that are accurate to sub-cellular scales for the raphe expression domain (intra-group registration accuracy = 3.5 µm; inter-group accuracy = 4.0 µm).
source: Our algorithms produce alignments that are accurate to sub-cellular scales for both the raphe expression domain (intra-group registration accuracy = 3.5 µm; inter-group accuracy = 4.0 µm) and the epiphysis expression domain (intra-group accuracy = 2.3 µm; inter-group accuracy = 2.5 µm).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the authors' experiments, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The registration algorithms produce alignments that are accurate to sub-cellular scales for the epiphysis expression domain (intra-group accuracy = 2.3 µm; inter-group accuracy = 2.5 µm).
source: Our algorithms produce alignments that are accurate to sub-cellular scales for both the raphe expression domain (intra-group registration accuracy = 3.5 µm; inter-group accuracy = 4.0 µm) and the epiphysis expression domain (intra-group accuracy = 2.3 µm; inter-group accuracy = 2.5 µm).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the authors' experiments, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (vmat2) is expressed in dopaminergic neurons of the telencephalon and diencephalon, noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus, and serotonergic neurons of the raphe nuclei.
source: Vmat2 is expressed in DA neurons of the telencephalon and diencephalon, NA neurons of the locus coeruleus, and 5-HT neurons of the raphe nuclei (Wen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wen et al., 2008, which provides external evidence for vmat2 expression patterns.

claim: Tyrosine hydroxylase (th) is expressed in dopaminergic neurons of the telencephalon and diencephalon and noradrenergic neurons of the locus coeruleus in zebrafish.
source: In zebrafish, th is expressed in DA neurons of the telencephalon and diencephalon and noradrenergic (NA) neurons of the locus coeruleus (Rink and Wullimann, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rink and Wullimann, 2002, which provides external evidence for th expression patterns in zebrafish.

claim: Tryptophan hydroxylase 2 (tph2) is expressed in serotonergic neurons of the epiphysis and the raphe nuclei.
source: Tph2 is expressed in 5-HT neurons of the epiphysis and the raphe nuclei(Teraoka et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Teraoka et al., 2004, which provides external evidence for tph2 expression patterns.

claim: All sites of co-expression (th and vmat2 in DA clusters; th and tph2 in the locus coeruleus and raphe nuclei) are accurately recapitulated when examining 2D slices from 3D reconstructions that have been co-registered using the authors' algorithms.
source: When we examine 2D slices from 3D reconstructions of th, vmat2, and tph2 that have been co-registered using our algorithms, all sites of co-expression (th and vmat2 in DA clusters; th and tph2 in the locus coeruleus and raphe nuclei) are accurately recapitulated (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C, which demonstrates the accuracy of the co-registration approach.

claim: The authors created 3D reference atlases for zebrafish brains at 2 and 3 dpf.
source: To enable quantification and analysis of gene expression based on anatomical context, we created 3D reference atlases for zebrafish brains at 2 and 3 dpf (Source code 1).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological contribution and is supported by the availability of the atlases as source code.

claim: Atlases were developed from 3D images generated by 2P excitation microscopy using embryos stained with green fluorescent Nissl stain.
source: Atlases were developed from 3D images generated by 2P excitation microscopy using embryos stained with green fluorescent Nissl stain.
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach to creating the atlases.

claim: Nissl stain is widely used to study neuromorphology.
source: This histological stain is widely used to study neuromorphology (Nissl, 1894; Kádár et al., 2009) and provides a convenient way to visualize general brain anatomy.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nissl, 1894 and Kádár et al., 2009, which provide external evidence for the use of Nissl stain in neuromorphology studies.

claim: Automated Correlation Analysis is based on an approach used for group comparisons in brain network studies.
source: In order to automatically detect regional differences in expression, we developed an Automated Correlation Analysis framework based on an approach used for group comparisons in brain network studies (Simpson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Simpson et al., 2013, which provides external evidence for the methodological basis of the Automated Correlation Analysis approach.

claim: A Pearson correlation coefficient is calculated between each wild-type and mutant embryo for every probe within all brain regions based on the intensities of corresponding voxels.
source: Following registration, we calculate a Pearson correlation coefficient between each wild-type and mutant embryo for every probe within all brain regions based on the intensities of corresponding voxels (Goshtasby, 2012).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach and is supported by a citation to Goshtasby, 2012.

claim: The p-value threshold for automated phenotyping was set at p<10−5, which gives a false discovery rate of 0.043.
source: Based on this analysis, we have set our p-value threshold at p<10−5, which gives a FDR of 0.043.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis of false discovery rates using a null data set, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: In the null data set, the mean effect size is less than 1.0 for all significance thresholds evaluated.
source: In the null data set, the mean effect size is less than 1.0 for all significance thresholds evaluated (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Including an effect size requirement (d > 1.0) for Automated Correlation Analysis reduces the false discovery rate at the selected p-value threshold from 0.043 to 0.020.
source: Therefore, we included an effect size requirement (d > 1.0) for Automated Correlation Analysis, further reducing the FDR at our selected p-value threshold from 0.043 to 0.020 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Automated deep-phenotyping of fezf2 mutants reveals two phenotypic hotspots: one in the ventral diencephalon and one in the telencephalon.
source: Aggregated difference images clearly show two phenotypic hotspots in fezf2 mutants: one in the ventral diencephalon and one in the telencephalon (Figure 3B, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Video 2.

claim: One of the phenotypic hotspots detected by Automated Correlation Analysis is in the ventral diencephalon, an area encompassing the preoptic area, ventral thalamus, hypothalamus, and ventral posterior tuberculum.
source: One of the phenotypic hotspots detected by Automated Correlation Analysis is in the ventral diencephalon, an area encompassing the preoptic area, ventral thalamus, hypothalamus, and ventral posterior tuberculum (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Previous reports indicate that fezf2 is essential for multiple neuronal subtypes in the ventral diencephalon, including dopaminergic, serotonergic, and GABAergic neurons.
source: This agrees with previous reports that fezf2 is essential for multiple neuronal subtypes in the ventral diencephalon, including DA (Rink and Guo, 2004; Levkowitz et al., 2003; Guo et al., 1999), 5-HT (Levkowitz et al., 2003; Rink and Guo, 2004), and GABAergic neurons (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Rink and Guo, 2004; Levkowitz et al., 2003; Guo et al., 1999; Yang et al., 2012) that provide external evidence for previously reported fezf2 functions.

claim: The authors' analysis shows significantly reduced correlation in one or more ventral diencephalic regions for the GABAergic markers distal-less homeobox 5a (dlx5a) and glutamate decarboxylase 1b (gad1b) and the dopaminergic markers th, vmat2, and orthopedia homeobox b (otpb).
source: We see significantly reduced correlation in one or more ventral diencephalic regions for the GABAergic markers distal-less homeobox 5a (dlx5a) and glutamate decarboxylase 1b (gad1b) and the DA markers th, vmat2, and orthopedia homeobox b (otpb) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Loss of dopaminergic markers is seen at both 2 and 3 dpf in fezf2 mutants.
source: Loss of DA markers is seen at both 2 and 3 dpf, while dlx5a and gad1b appear to partially recover by 3 dpf (Supplementary file 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting for the first time that the GABAergic phenotype in fezf2 mutants may be transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: dlx5a and gad1b appear to partially recover by 3 dpf in fezf2 mutants, suggesting for the first time that the GABAergic phenotype in fezf2 mutants may be transient.
source: Loss of DA markers is seen at both 2 and 3 dpf, while dlx5a and gad1b appear to partially recover by 3 dpf (Supplementary file 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), suggesting for the first time that the GABAergic phenotype in fezf2 mutants may be transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B, and represents a novel finding from the authors' analysis.

claim: Most fezf2 diencephalic deficits are restricted to a subset of the expression domains for a given probe.
source: Most fezf2 diencephalic deficits are restricted to a subset of the expression domains for a given probe.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of multiple probes and is supported by specific examples provided in the text.

claim: otpb is lost in the ventral posterior tuberculum and posterior hypothalamus in fezf2 mutants, but remains largely unchanged in the anterior hypothalamus and other regions of the diencephalon.
source: For example, although otpb (a homeodomain protein essential for specification of subsets of neuroendocrine cells and DA neurons) is lost in the ventral posterior tuberculum and posterior hypothalamus, it remains largely unchanged in the anterior hypothalamus and other regions of the diencephalon (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,G,H.

claim: th expression is significantly reduced in the dopaminergic clusters of the ventral posterior tuberculum and hypothalamus in fezf2 mutants, with posterior clusters appearing to be more strongly affected than anterior clusters.
source: Similarly, th expression is significantly reduced in the DA clusters of the ventral posterior tuberculum and hypothalamus, with posterior clusters appearing to be more strongly affected than anterior clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Subdomain-specific defects in otpb and th have been characterized in detail in fezf2m808 mutants, providing validation for the authors' approach to automated phenotyping.
source: These subdomain-specific defects in otpb and th have been characterized in detail in fezf2m808 mutants (Rink and Guo, 2004; Blechman et al., 2007), providing validation for our approach to automated phenotyping.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rink and Guo, 2004 and Blechman et al., 2007, which provide external evidence for previously reported phenotypes that match the authors' findings.

claim: The early developmental expression pattern of fezf2 has been reported to be normal in fezf2m808 mutants, but the authors' analysis shows significant alterations in the ventral diencephalon and other regions.
source: The early developmental expression pattern of fezf2 has been reported to be normal in fezf2m808 mutants (Levkowitz et al., 2003), but our analysis shows significant alterations in the ventral diencephalon and other regions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Levkowitz et al., 2003 (which reported normal expression) and the authors' own data shown in Figure 3A (which shows alterations).

claim: Visualization of fezf2 using maximum intensity projections reveals that virtually all expression domains are altered in fezf2 mutants.
source: Visualization of fezf2 using MIPs reveals that virtually all expression domains are altered (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No other probe in the authors' library shows such widespread disruption as fezf2.
source: No other probe in our library shows such widespread disruption (Supplementary file 2), suggesting fezf2 plays a critical role in regulating its own expression either directly or via feedback from downstream transcriptional targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 2 and represents an inference about fezf2's role in regulating its own expression.

claim: In the posterior hypothalamus of wild-type embryos, fezf2 is expressed in a T-shaped pattern running along the midline and spreading into the lateral hypothalamus.
source: In the posterior hypothalamus of wild-type embryos, fezf2 is expressed in a T-shaped pattern running along the midline and spreading into the lateral hypothalamus (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: When otpb and th are virtually co-registered with fezf2, they are located in an anterior/lateral position relative to fezf2 in the posterior hypothalamus.
source: When otpb and th are virtually co-registered with fezf2, they are located in an anterior/lateral position relative to fezf2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: This distinctive arrangement of fezf2 and otpb in the posterior hypothalamus has been described previously using two-color fluorescent in situ hybridization.
source: This distinctive arrangement of fezf2 and otpb in the posterior hypothalamus has been described previously using two-color fluorescent in situ hybridization (Wolf and Ryu, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wolf and Ryu, 2013, which provides external evidence for the spatial relationship between fezf2 and otpb.

claim: In fezf2 mutants, fezf2 expression is lost along the midline while simultaneously expanding laterally and anteriorly into regions normally expressing otpb and th.
source: In fezf2 mutants, fezf2 expression is lost along the midline while simultaneously expanding laterally and anteriorly into regions normally expressing otpb and th (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Previous work shows that fezf2 is required for expression of otpb and the closely related otpa.
source: Previous work shows that fezf2 is required for expression of otpb and the closely related otpa.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of previous studies, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Otp genes act as negative regulators of fezf2.
source: Otp genes in turn act as negative regulators of fezf2 (Yang et al., 2012; Wolf and Ryu, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2012 and Wolf and Ryu, 2013, which provide external evidence for the regulatory relationship between otp and fezf2.

claim: Otp genes are essential for development of dopaminergic neurons in the diencephalon.
source: Since otp genes are essential for development of DA neurons in the diencephalon (Fernandes et al., 2013; Ryu et al., 2007), it is not surprising that th expression is lost in this region of fezf2 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fernandes et al., 2013 and Ryu et al., 2007, which provide external evidence for the role of otp genes in dopaminergic neuron development.

claim: Automated phenotyping shows that somatostatin-expressing neurons (sst1.1) are lost in the ventral diencephalon of fezf2 mutants.
source: Automated phenotyping also shows that somatostatin-expressing neurons (sst1.1) are lost in the ventral diencephalon.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' automated phenotyping analysis.

claim: Deficits in sst1.1 expression in fezf2 mutants are limited to a small bilateral cluster located between the hypothalamus and the ventral thalamus/ventral posterior tuberculum.
source: Although distinct clusters of sst1.1 neurons are present in many regions, deficits in fezf2 mutants are limited to a small bilateral cluster located between the hypothalamus and the ventral thalamus/ventral posterior tuberculum (Figures 3C and 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3C and 4D.

claim: Affected sst1.1 clusters partially overlap with optb in the hypothalamus and are either intermingled with or located just lateral to dopaminergic clusters.
source: Virtual co-expression analysis shows that affected sst1.1 clusters partially overlap with optb in the hypothalamus and are either intermingled with or located just lateral to DA clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: In the context of the zebrafish hindbrain, otp is required for the development of sst1.1 neurons.
source: As previously noted, fezf2 is required for otp expression in the ventral diencephalon (Blechman et al., 2007; Wolf and Ryu, 2013) and—at least in the context of the zebrafish hindbrain—otp is required for the development of sst1.1 neurons (Fernandes et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Blechman et al., 2007, Wolf and Ryu, 2013, and Fernandes et al., 2013, which provide external evidence for the regulatory relationships between fezf2, otp, and sst1.1.

claim: A previous publication found no sst1.1 defects in fezf2 mutants, but this conclusion was likely based on the strongly-expressing sst1.1 clusters in the anterior hypothalamus, which appear normal in the authors' analysis.
source: Although a previous publication found no sst1.1 defects in fezf2 mutants (Blechman et al., 2007), this conclusion was likely based on the strongly-expressing sst1.1 clusters in the anterior hypothalamus, which appear normal in our analysis (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blechman et al., 2007 and the authors' own data shown in Figure 3A,C, along with an inference about why the previous study missed the phenotype.

claim: The second phenotypic hotspot in fezf2 mutants is the telencephalon.
source: The second phenotypic hotspot in fezf2 mutants is the telencephalon (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Previous studies of fezf2 phenotypes report that morphology and patterning of the telencephalon is normal during early development.
source: Surprisingly, previous studies of fezf2 phenotypes report that morphology and patterning of the telencephalon is normal during early development.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of previous studies, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: The size and number of th-expressing dopaminergic cells in the telencephalon is normal in fezf2 mutants during the first 2 weeks of development.
source: In contrast to the diencephalon, the size and number of th-expressing DA cells in the telencephalon is normal in mutants during the first 2 weeks of development (Guo et al., 1999; Levkowitz et al., 2003; Rink and Guo, 2004), although TH immunoreactive processes in the subpallium are reduced at later stages (Rink and Guo, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 1999, Levkowitz et al., 2003, and Rink and Guo, 2004, which provide external evidence for the telencephalic dopaminergic phenotype in fezf2 mutants.

claim: TH immunoreactive processes in the subpallium are reduced at later stages in fezf2 mutants.
source: In contrast to the diencephalon, the size and number of th-expressing DA cells in the telencephalon is normal in mutants during the first 2 weeks of development (Guo et al., 1999; Levkowitz et al., 2003; Rink and Guo, 2004), although TH immunoreactive processes in the subpallium are reduced at later stages (Rink and Guo, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rink and Guo, 2004, which provides external evidence for the later-stage phenotype.

claim: Telencephalic expression of the GABAergic marker gad1b is reported to be normal in fezf2 deficient embryos.
source: Similarly, telencephalic expression of the GABAergic marker gad1b is reported to be normal in fezf2 deficient embryos (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2012, which provides external evidence for the GABAergic phenotype in fezf2 mutants.

claim: The authors' Automated Correlation Analysis shows dopaminergic markers (th, otpb, vmat2) in the telencephalon are essentially normal in fezf2 mutants, although there may be small changes in th expression at 3 dpf.
source: Consistent with these studies, our Automated Correlation Analysis shows DA markers (th, otpb, vmat2) in the telencephalon are essentially normal, although there may be small changes in th expression at 3 dpf (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GABAergic markers (dlx5a, gad1b) and glutamatergic markers (vglut1, vglut2.2) show reduced correlation in the telencephalon of fezf2 mutants.
source: In contrast, GABAergic markers (dlx5a, gad1b) and glutamatergic markers [vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (vglut1), vglut2.2] show reduced correlation in the telencephalon.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' Automated Correlation Analysis.

claim: Maximum intensity projections confirm that GABAergic and glutamatergic markers show areas of significant difference in the telencephalon of fezf2 mutants, while dopaminergic markers remain unaffected.
source: MIPs confirm that GABAergic and glutamatergic markers show areas of significant difference in the telencephalon, while DA markers remain unaffected (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Glutamatergic neurons exhibit a striking reduction in the telencephalon at 2 and 3 dpf in fezf2 mutants.
source: Glutamatergic neurons exhibit a striking reduction in the telencephalon at 2 and 3 dpf while the GABAergic phenotype is more complex and appears to encompass both areas of reduced and increased expression.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of glutamatergic markers in fezf2 mutants.

claim: The GABAergic phenotype in the telencephalon of fezf2 mutants is more complex and appears to encompass both areas of reduced and increased expression.
source: Glutamatergic neurons exhibit a striking reduction in the telencephalon at 2 and 3 dpf while the GABAergic phenotype is more complex and appears to encompass both areas of reduced and increased expression.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of GABAergic markers in fezf2 mutants.

claim: Dopaminergic markers, expressed in bilateral domains in the telencephalon, are largely unaltered in fezf2 mutants.
source: DA markers, expressed in bilateral domains in the telencephalon, are largely unaltered in fezf2 mutants (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplements 1B and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplements 1B and 2.

claim: Defects in GABAergic markers (dlx5a, gad1b) in the telencephalon are subtle and appear to be driven by alterations in 3D shape rather than by a change in volume.
source: Defects in GABAergic markers (dlx5a, gad1b) are subtle and appear to be driven by alterations in 3D shape rather than by a change in volume (Figure 5B,E; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Volume measurements from 3D segmentations of dlx5a-stained embryos show no significant difference in spite of clear changes in overall shape.
source: This impression is confirmed by quantifying 3D segmentations from dlx5a-stained embryos. Volume measurements show no significant difference in spite of clear changes in overall shape (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: GABAergic markers exhibit a small lateral shift away from the midline ventricle in fezf2 mutants at 2 and 3 dpf.
source: 2D sections through the pallium show that GABAergic markers exhibit a small lateral shift away from the midline ventricle in mutants at 2 and 3 dpf (Figure 5B,E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Gad1b appears to be slightly reduced in the posterior region of the pallium in fezf2 mutants.
source: Gad1b also appears to be slightly reduced in the posterior region of the pallium (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Glutamatergic defects in the telencephalon are highly pronounced when examined in slices and 3D segmentations and clearly reflect a substantial decrease in volume.
source: In contrast to the GABAergic phenotype, glutamatergic defects in the telencephalon are highly pronounced when examined in slices and 3D segmentations and clearly reflect a substantial decrease in volume (Figure 5C,F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C,F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Video 3.

claim: Vglut1 expression is primarily restricted to the pallium.
source: Vglut1 expression is primarily restricted to the pallium, while vglut2.2 is more broadly expressed throughout the pallium, subpallium, and olfactory bulb (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vglut2.2 is more broadly expressed throughout the pallium, subpallium, and olfactory bulb.
source: Vglut1 expression is primarily restricted to the pallium, while vglut2.2 is more broadly expressed throughout the pallium, subpallium, and olfactory bulb (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: 2D slices and volume measurements from 3D segmentations confirm that both vglut1 and vglut2.2 are significantly reduced in fezf2 mutants, with loss of the pallial glutamatergic population being particularly dramatic.
source: 2D slices and volume measurements from 3D segmentations confirm that both markers are significantly reduced in fezf2 mutants, with loss of the pallial glutamatergic population being particularly dramatic.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of 2D slices and 3D segmentations.

claim: fezf2 mutants show a reduction in telencephalic tbr1b, a T-box transcription factor that plays an essential role in specifying glutamatergic pyramidal neurons in the mammalian neocortex.
source: In addition to deficits in vglut genes—which mark mature glutamatergic populations—mutants show a reduction in telencephalic tbr1b, a T-box transcription factor that plays an essential role in specifying glutamatergic pyramidal neurons in the mammalian neocortex (Englund et al., 2005; Hevner et al., 2006) (Figure 5—figure supplements 1E and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Englund et al., 2005 and Hevner et al., 2006, and by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1E and 2.

claim: Similar to dlx5a and gad1b, tbr1b undergoes a slight lateral shift away from the telencephalic midline ventricle in fezf2 mutants.
source: Similar to dlx5a and gad1b, tbr1b undergoes a slight lateral shift away from the telencephalic midline ventricle.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of tbr1b expression patterns.

claim: The authors' findings represent the first evidence that fezf2 is required for development of glutamatergic neurons in the zebrafish telencephalon.
source: Our findings represent the first evidence that fezf2 is required for development of glutamatergic neurons in the zebrafish telencephalon.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' novel findings and their knowledge of the existing literature.

claim: Many other probes show reduced correlation in the telencephalon of fezf2 mutants, including markers of multipotent progenitor subpopulations (aslc1a, eomesa, neurog1, zic2a), a marker of astrocytic and glycinergic differentiation (glyt1), and a transcription factor broadly expressed within the zebrafish telencephalon (emx3).
source: In addition to GABAergic and glutamatergic defects, many other probes show reduced correlation in the telencephalon (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 2). These include markers of multipotent progenitor subpopulations (aslc1a, Figure 5D; eomesa, neurog1, zic2a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G–I) (Houtmeyers et al., 2013; Wilkinson et al., 2013; Englund et al., 2005), a marker of astrocytic and glycinergic differentiation (glyt1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) (Betz et al., 2006), and a transcription factor broadly expressed within the zebrafish telencephalon (emx3, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) (Viktorin et al., 2009; Ganz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, Supplementary file 2, Figure 5D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,F,G–I, along with citations to relevant literature.

claim: The fezf2 expression domain itself is highly disorganized in mutants in the telencephalon.
source: As in the diencephalon, the fezf2 expression domain itself is highly disorganized in mutants (Figure 5—figure supplements 1A and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1A and 2.

claim: Many markers are compressed along the dorsoventral axis of the telencephalon in fezf2 mutants, a change that is sometimes accompanied by reduced volume.
source: Many markers are compressed along the dorsoventral axis of the telencephalon in mutants, a change that is sometimes accompanied by reduced volume (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; note reduction in emx3 and eomesa, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Dorsoventral compression is most evident in markers with strong midline ventricle expression such as ascl1a.
source: Dorsoventral compression is most evident in markers with strong midline ventricle expression such as ascl1a (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Loss of expression in fezf2 mutants is particularly pronounced in the pallium, as seen when markers broadly expressed in the pallium and subpallium (emx3, tbr1b) are co-registered with markers that are more restricted to the subpallium (dlx5a, gad1b).
source: When loss of expression occurs it is particularly pronounced in the pallium, as seen when markers broadly expressed in the pallium and subpallium (emx3, tbr1b) are co-registered with markers that are more restricted to the subpallium (dlx5a, gad1b) (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Many diencephalic expression domains located in close proximity to the telencephalon undergo an anterior/ventral shift in fezf2 mutants.
source: Lastly, many diencephalic expression domains located in close proximity to the telencephalon undergo an anterior/ventral shift.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' analysis of multiple markers.

claim: The anterior/ventral shift in diencephalic expression domains is evident in gad1b, dlx5a, ascl1a, and neurog1.
source: This shift is evident in gad1b (Figures 4B and 5E), dlx5a (Figure 5B), ascl1a (Figure 5D), and neurog1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4B, 5E, 5B, 5D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The size of the telencephalon (particularly the pallium) may be reduced in fezf2 mutants, resulting in a concomitant anterior/ventral shift in neighboring diencephalic domains when embryos are co-registered.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest the size of the telencephalon (particularly the pallium) may be reduced in fezf2 mutants, resulting in a concomitant anterior/ventral shift in neighboring diencephalic domains when embryos are co-registered.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the authors' observations of multiple markers and expression patterns.

claim: Volume measurements from manual 3D segmentations of Nissl-stained embryos showed a highly significant reduction in overall telencephalic size in fezf2 mutants.
source: Volume measurements showed a highly significant reduction in overall telencephalic size in fezf2 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The brain ventricle of the dorsal telencephalon is noticeably larger in fezf2 mutants based on sections through Nissl-stained images.
source: Additionally, the brain ventricle of the dorsal telencephalon is noticeably larger in mutants based on sections through Nissl-stained images (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Automated quantitative phenotyping approaches will be invaluable for characterizing the numerous new lines being developed using advanced genome editing techniques.
source: Automated quantitative phenotyping approaches like this will be invaluable for characterizing the numerous new lines being developed using advanced genome editing techniques.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' speculation about the future utility of their approach.

claim: 3D datasets are essential for understanding developmental patterning and for systems-level analysis of gene regulatory networks and neural circuits.
source: 3D datasets are essential for understanding developmental patterning and for systems-level analysis of gene regulatory networks and neural circuits.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the importance of 3D data in developmental biology.

claim: Published techniques for automated 3D analysis of gene expression in zebrafish are limited to fluorescent readouts and optical sectioning approaches.
source: Published techniques for automated 3D analysis of gene expression in zebrafish are limited to fluorescent readouts and optical sectioning approaches (Ronneberger et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ronneberger et al., 2012, which provides external evidence for the limitations of existing techniques.

claim: Chromogenic WISH staining offers a complementary approach to 3D phenotyping.
source: Chromogenic WISH staining offers a complementary approach to 3D phenotyping.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' inference about the advantages of chromogenic WISH relative to fluorescent approaches.

claim: Photobleaching and quenching are not a concern with chromogenic WISH stains.
source: Photobleaching and quenching are not a concern, stains are extremely high-contrast (allowing for higher-throughput imaging) and stable for years, and protocols are well-established, robust, inexpensive, and have been fully automated (Hauptmann, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the properties of chromogenic stains, supported by a citation to Hauptmann, 2015.

claim: Chromogenic WISH stains are extremely high-contrast, allowing for higher-throughput imaging.
source: Photobleaching and quenching are not a concern, stains are extremely high-contrast (allowing for higher-throughput imaging) and stable for years, and protocols are well-established, robust, inexpensive, and have been fully automated (Hauptmann, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the properties of chromogenic stains, supported by a citation to Hauptmann, 2015.

claim: Chromogenic WISH stains are stable for years.
source: Photobleaching and quenching are not a concern, stains are extremely high-contrast (allowing for higher-throughput imaging) and stable for years, and protocols are well-established, robust, inexpensive, and have been fully automated (Hauptmann, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the properties of chromogenic stains, supported by a citation to Hauptmann, 2015.

claim: Chromogenic WISH protocols are well-established, robust, inexpensive, and have been fully automated.
source: Photobleaching and quenching are not a concern, stains are extremely high-contrast (allowing for higher-throughput imaging) and stable for years, and protocols are well-established, robust, inexpensive, and have been fully automated (Hauptmann, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about chromogenic WISH protocols, supported by a citation to Hauptmann, 2015.

claim: Using deep phenotyping to analyze zebrafish fezf2 mutants, the authors have detected several overlooked deficits.
source: Using deep phenotyping to analyze zebrafish fezf2 mutants, we have detected several overlooked deficits.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' experimental findings.

claim: The authors show for the first time that fezf2 mutants exhibit defects in glutamatergic neurogenesis in the telencephalon and that this phenotype is already present at 2 dpf.
source: We show for the first time that mutants exhibit defects in glutamatergic neurogenesis in the telencephalon and that this phenotype is already present at 2 dpf.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' novel findings from their deep phenotyping analysis.

claim: The authors' findings reveal unsuspected commonalities between fezf2 function in fish and mammals and suggest an evolutionarily conserved role in glutamatergic development, particularly in the dorsal telencephalon.
source: These data reveal unsuspected commonalities between fezf2 function in fish and mammals and suggest an evolutionarily conserved role in glutamatergic development, particularly in the dorsal telencephalon.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the authors' findings and their comparison with mammalian phenotypes.

claim: Zebrafish fezf2 mutants are characterized by diencephalic deficits in dopaminergic, serotonergic, and GABAergic populations.
source: Zebrafish mutants are characterized by diencephalic deficits in DA, 5-HT, and GABAergic populations, while knockout mice display telencephalic deficits in cortical glutamatergic projection neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of previously reported zebrafish phenotypes.

claim: Fezf2 knockout mice display telencephalic deficits in cortical glutamatergic projection neurons.
source: Zebrafish mutants are characterized by diencephalic deficits in DA, 5-HT, and GABAergic populations, while knockout mice display telencephalic deficits in cortical glutamatergic projection neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of previously reported mouse phenotypes.

claim: In mice, ectopic expression of Fezf2 in neural progenitor populations that normally give rise to GABAergic neurons redirects them to a glutamatergic fate.
source: In mice, ectopic expression of Fezf2 in neural progenitor populations that normally give rise to GABAergic neurons redirects them to a glutamatergic fate (Rouaux and Arlotta, 2010; Zuccotti et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rouaux and Arlotta, 2010 and Zuccotti et al., 2014, which provide external evidence for Fezf2's role in cell fate specification in mice.

claim: Fezf2 has been shown to promote glutamatergic corticospinal motor neuron identity and repress GABAergic identity in mammalian cells by activating Vglut1 and repressing Gad1.
source: Consistent with this, Fezf2 has been shown to promote glutamatergic corticospinal motor neuron identity and repress GABAergic identity in mammalian cells by activating Vglut1 and repressing Gad1 (Lodato et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lodato et al., 2014, which provides external evidence for Fezf2's molecular mechanisms in mammals.

claim: Overexpression of fezf2 during early zebrafish development results in increased dopaminergic neurons in the ventral diencephalon.
source: In contrast, overexpression of fezf2 during early zebrafish development results in increased DA neurons in the ventral diencephalon (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2012, which provides external evidence for the effects of fezf2 overexpression in zebrafish.

claim: Until now, no fezf2 glutamatergic defects have been described in zebrafish.
source: Until now, no fezf2 glutamatergic defects have been described in zebrafish, raising the possibility that fezf2 has assumed novel functions in the mammalian telencephalon.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the existing literature.

claim: Based on the authors' findings, it seems likely fezf2 actually has a longstanding role in telencephalic glutamatergic differentiation predating the divergence of teleosts and tetraopods.
source: Based on our findings, it seems likely fezf2 actually has a longstanding role in telencephalic glutamatergic differentiation predating the divergence of teleosts and tetraopods.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the authors' findings and their implications for evolutionary conservation.

claim: Glutamatergic populations are most strongly affected in the pallium of fezf2 mutants, the same region of the telencephalon from which the mammalian neocortex is derived.
source: Significantly, glutamatergic populations are most strongly affected in the pallium of fezf2 mutants, the same region of the telencephalon from which the mammalian neocortex is derived.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' findings and their knowledge of telencephalon evolution.

claim: The authors' findings bring fezf2 defects during early zebrafish development into closer agreement with phenotypes described in adult fish.
source: In addition to revealing a common role for fezf2 in glutamatergic neurogenesis, our findings bring fezf2 defects during early zebrafish development into closer agreement with phenotypes described in adult fish.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the authors' findings and their comparison with previously reported adult phenotypes.

claim: Adult fezf2 mutants have strikingly smaller telencephalons, although gross morphological changes are not apparent even at 2 weeks post fertilization.
source: Recently it has been reported that adult fezf2 mutants have strikingly smaller telencephalons, although gross morphological changes are not apparent even at 2 weeks post fertilization (Berberoglu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berberoglu et al., 2014, which provides external evidence for the adult telencephalon phenotype.

claim: Telencephalic reduction in adult fezf2 mutants is accompanied by distortions in fezf2 expression and enlargement of the dorsal telencephalon ventricle.
source: Telencephalic reduction is accompanied by distortions in fezf2 expression and enlargement of the dorsal telencephalon ventricle.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of previously reported adult phenotypes.

claim: Reduced telencephalic size, altered fezf2 expression, and ventricular enlargement is the same constellation of phenotypes the authors detect at 2 dpf using deep-phenotyping, although all deficits are far less pronounced at this early stage.
source: Reduced telencephalic size, altered fezf2 expression, and ventricular enlargement is the same constellation of phenotypes we detect at 2 dpf using deep-phenotyping, although all deficits are far less pronounced at this early stage and would be difficult to detect without quantitative 3D approaches.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' findings and their comparison with adult phenotypes.

claim: Previous studies have reported decreased neurite complexity and increased numbers of neural stem cells in the dorsal telencephalon of adult fezf2 mutants, suggesting a failure of maturation and differentiation.
source: Previous studies have also reported decreased neurite complexity and increased numbers of neural stem cells in the dorsal telencephalon of adult fezf2 mutants, suggesting a failure of maturation and differentiation (Berberoglu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Berberoglu et al., 2014, which provides external evidence for the adult neural stem cell phenotype.

claim: Pluripotent progenitor markers (ascl1a, ascl1b, neurog1) are not significantly reduced in the fezf2 mutant pallium, while markers of some postmitotic subtypes (tbr1b, vglut1, vglut2.2) undergo a substantial reduction.
source: This interpretation is supported by our finding that pluripotent progenitor markers (ascl1a, ascl1b, neurog1) are not significantly reduced in the fezf2 mutant pallium, while markers of some postmitotic subtypes (tbr1b, vglut1, vglut2.2) undergo a substantial reduction (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: All procedures on live animals were approved by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Committee on Animal Care.
source: All procedures on live animals were approved by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Committee on Animal Care.
evidence: This claim is a statement of ethical compliance.

claim: Zebrafish bearing the fezf2m808 mutation were a generous gift of S Guo, UCSF, San Francisco, CA.
source: Zebrafish bearing the fezf2m808 mutation (also known as too few; tofm808; RRID:ZFIN_ZDB-ALT-980520-28) were a generous gift of S Guo, UCSF, San Francisco, CA (Rink and Guo, 2004).
evidence: This claim is a statement of the source of the mutant fish line, supported by a citation to Rink and Guo, 2004.

claim: Homozygous mutant fezf2m808 embryos and age-matched wild-type siblings were obtained by crossing heterozygous fezf2 adults that had previously been backcrossed to the TAB14 wild-type background.
source: Homozygous mutant fezf2m808 embryos and age-matched wild-type siblings were obtained by crossing heterozygous fezf2 adults that had previously been backcrossed to the TAB14 wild-type background (Zebrafish International Resource Center catalog #ZL1438).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' experimental approach to generating mutant and wild-type embryos.

claim: 0.2 mM 1-Phenyl-2-thiourea (PTU) was added to the embryo medium to inhibit melanogenesis.
source: In all experiments, 0.2 mM 1-Phenyl-2-thiourea (PTU) was added to the embryo medium to inhibit melanogenesis (Karlsson et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' experimental protocol, supported by a citation to Karlsson et al., 2001.

claim: The authors used the Derived Cleaved Amplified Polymorphic Sequences (dCAPS) method to detect the fezf2m808 mutation.
source: Embryonic and adult zebrafish were genotyped using the Derived Cleaved Amplified Polymorphic Sequences (dCAPS) method to detect the fezf2m808 mutation (Yanagisawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' genotyping method, supported by a citation to Yanagisawa et al., 2003.

claim: The authors generated a custom in situ probe library by using RT-PCR to amplify marker genes of interest from total RNA isolated and pooled from zebrafish embryos between 1–6 dpf.
source: We generated a custom in situ probe library by using RT-PCR to amplify marker genes of interest from total RNA isolated and pooled from zebrafish embryos between 1–6 dpf (see Supplementary file 1 for genes, probe lengths, and RT-PCR primer pairs).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach to generating in situ probes.

claim: Whole-mount in situ hybridization (WISH) was performed essentially as described by Thisse and Thisse, 2008, but with several important modifications.
source: Whole-mount in situ hybridization (WISH) was performed essentially as described (Thisse and Thisse, 2008), but with several important modifications that minimize physical distortions to fixed embryos during high temperature hybridization steps, optimize the robustness of the staining reaction, and increase the stability of stained samples during clearing and tomographic imaging steps.
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach, supported by a citation to Thisse and Thisse, 2008.

claim: The authors' OPT platform uses a broadband Tungsten-Halogen lamp for illumination.
source: A broadband Tungsten-Halogen lamp (#QTH10; Thorlabs, Newton, NJ) is used for illumination.
evidence: This claim describes a component of the authors' OPT platform.

claim: The authors' OPT platform uses a high-speed CCD camera (Prosilica GX 1050C) for acquisition.
source: A high-speed CCD camera (Prosilica GX 1050C; Allied Vision Technologies, Stadtroda, Germany) is used for acquisition.
evidence: This claim describes a component of the authors' OPT platform.

claim: Average handling time per embryo is 55.0 ± 2.9 s when loading and unloading is done manually.
source: Average handling time per embryo is 55.0 ± 2.9 s when loading and unloading is done manually (embryo loading: 19.4 ± 2.1s; image acquisition and data transfer: 18.0 ± 0.7s; embryo unloading: 17.6 ± 3.0).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the authors' experiments.

claim: The alignment and reconstruction takes approximately 11 minutes per embryo to run on a 2.6 GHz hexa-core processor standard workstation.
source: The alignment and reconstruction takes ~11 min per embryo to run on a 2.6 GHz hexa-core processor standard workstation and the reconstructed image has a size of 512x512 × 512 voxels.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from the authors' computational pipeline.

claim: The reconstructed image has a size of 512x512 × 512 voxels.
source: The alignment and reconstruction takes ~11 min per embryo to run on a 2.6 GHz hexa-core processor standard workstation and the reconstructed image has a size of 512x512 × 512 voxels.
evidence: This claim describes a technical specification of the authors' reconstruction pipeline.

claim: All registrations are done with the toolbox elastix and MATLAB Image Processing Toolbox.
source: All registrations discussed below are done with the toolbox elastix (RRID:SCR_009619) (Klein et al., 2010; Shamonin et al., 2013) and MATLAB Image Processing Toolbox (Release R2015b; MathWorks, Natick, MA).
evidence: This claim describes the software tools used by the authors, supported by citations to Klein et al., 2010 and Shamonin et al., 2013.

claim: A rigid transform consists of only translation and rotation.
source: A rigid transform consists of only translation and rotation.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about image registration transforms.

claim: The similarity transform consists of translation, rotation, and isotropic scaling.
source: The similarity transform consists of translation, rotation, and isotropic scaling.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about image registration transforms.

claim: The affine transformation consists of translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing.
source: The affine transformation consists of translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about image registration transforms.

claim: The B-spline transform is a deformable transform where a deformation field is modelled using B-splines.
source: The B-spline transform is a deformable transform where a deformation field is modelled using B-splines.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about image registration transforms.

claim: The authors use a local rigidity penalty term developed for medical image registration in all deformable registrations.
source: We use a local rigidity penalty term developed for medical image registration in all deformable registrations (Staring et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach, supported by a citation to Staring et al., 2007.

claim: The measure of similarity used in all registrations is normalized correlation, which is computed using elastix.
source: The measure of similarity used in all registrations is normalized correlation, which is computed using elastix (Klein et al., 2010; Shamonin et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach, supported by citations to Klein et al., 2010 and Shamonin et al., 2013.

claim: Manual segmentation of the brain regions was done using the software TurtleSeg 1.3.
source: Manual segmentation of the brain regions was done using the software TurtleSeg 1.3 (Oxipita, Vancouver, Canada; RRID:SCR_002605) (Top et al., 2011, Top et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach, supported by citations to Top et al., 2011 and Top et al., 2010.

claim: Anatomical segmentation was done manually following established zebrafish brain nomenclature and with the aid of the Atlas of Early Zebrafish Brain Development and the ViBE-Z 3D atlas.
source: Anatomical segmentation was done manually following established zebrafish brain nomenclature and with the aid of the Atlas of Early Zebrafish Brain Development (Mueller and Wullimann, 2015) and the ViBE-Z 3D atlas (RRID:SCR_005895; http://vibez.informatik.uni-freiburg.de/) (Ronneberger et al., 2012; Rath et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach, supported by citations to Mueller and Wullimann, 2015, Ronneberger et al., 2012, and Rath et al., 2012.

claim: The authors' 2 and 3 dpf 3D anatomical brain atlases comprise 22 different brain regions located within the telencephalon, diencephalon, midbrain, and hindbrain.
source: Our 2 and 3 dpf 3D anatomical brain atlases comprise 22 different brain regions located within the telencephalon, diencephalon, midbrain, and hindbrain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' anatomical atlases, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Automated Correlation Analysis and other automated phenotyping steps are carried out on results from the final deformable registration step.
source: Automated Correlation Analysis and other automated phenotyping steps (Figure 3A–C) are carried out on results from the final deformable registration step.
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological workflow.

claim: Analysis is done in MATLAB on 2× downsampled data from the red channel, where the WISH signal is strongest.
source: Analysis is done in MATLAB on 2× downsampled data from the red channel, where the WISH signal is strongest.
evidence: This claim describes the authors' methodological approach.

claim: The Mann-Whitney U test is used to assess if intra-group correlations are significantly larger than inter-group correlations (p<1×10−5).
source: The Mann-Whitney U test is used to assess if intra-group correlations (wild-type vs. wild-type and mutant vs. mutant) are significantly larger than inter-group (wild-type vs. mutant) correlations (p<1×10−5).
evidence: This claim describes the authors' statistical approach.

claim: A voxel is considered to be significantly increased or decreased if the p-value from the Mann-Whitney U test is below 0.5 × 10−3.
source: A voxel is considered to be significantly increased or decreased if the p-value from the Mann-Whitney U is below 0.5 × 10−3.
evidence: This claim describes the authors' statistical threshold for voxelwise analysis.

claim: Core source code for image reconstruction and registration, along with brain atlases and sample data files, are available online.
source: Core source code for image reconstruction and registration (https://github.com/aallalou/OPT-InSitu-Toolbox; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/OPT-InSitu-Toolbox) (Allalou, 2017), along with brain atlases (Source code 1, see below) and sample data files (Source code 2, see below), are available online.
evidence: This claim describes the availability of the authors' computational tools and data.
